paras: The Cleves town hall attack and threatened attack on Coal City was a racial clash at Cleves, Ohio, early on April 9, 1903, in which a band of nearly fifty Black men was reported to have stoned and fired on a hall where young white people were dancing, white men chased them with revolvers, and a patrol was posted to keep "indignant whites" from attacking "the negro settlement at Coal City." Several white dancers and one Black man were slightly hurt, and no attack on Coal City was reported. The story spread as a short wire item under headlines that called the Black attackers a "mob" and "toughs," while the threatened white reprisal appeared only as its last sentence.

Cleves lay six miles from Lawrenceburg, Indiana, where both surviving accounts were datelined. The Indianapolis Journal headed its report "Culmination of a Race War" and said the affair was "the result of a race war," but it did not describe what had gone before. No paper located Coal City or described the settlement beyond calling it "the negro settlement," or in one reprint the "colored settlement."

According to the Indianapolis Journal, at about 1:30 in the morning a party of "merrymakers" was driven from a "reputable dance hall" by a rain of boulders on its sides and roof. Young men who ran outside were met by stones and bullets from a band of nearly fifty Black men. The wire dispatch said the attackers carried "various weapons" and wrecked the walls, roof and windows of the town hall with boulders, clubs and bullets, slightly injuring several of the dancers.

In the wire's account, white men with drawn revolvers then chased the attackers in a running fight through the town in which many shots were fired. One Black man was slightly wounded but escaped; the dispatch did not say who fired the shot that hit him. The Indianapolis Journal instead said police pursued the band a short distance and that none of its members was taken or recognized. The wire closed by reporting that a patrol was preventing an attack by "indignant whites" on the Black settlement at Coal City.

No arrests were reported, since by the Indianapolis Journal's account no attacker was recognized. The coverage contains no later report on the patrol, on Coal City, or on any inquiry into the shooting.

The Lawrenceburg dispatch ran on April 10 in the Louisville Courier-Journal, the Montgomery Advertiser and the Wheeling Register. The same day it appeared in the Birmingham Age-Herald, the Rock Island Argus and the St. Louis Republic, and in the Omaha Daily Bee under the headline "Blacks Demolish City Hall." Weeklies carried it into late April, re-dated to April 10 or 11, including the Bryan Morning Eagle and The Caucasian, both under "Negro Toughs," the Willmar Tribune under "Race Troubles" and the Wausau Pilot under "Negro Mob Wrecks Hall."

Most headlines led with the attack on the whites, as in the Montgomery Advertiser's "Negroes on War Path," and the wire's own phrase for the attackers was "the black mob." The Courier-Journal was the only paper found that headlined the other side of the story, "Attack on Negro Settlement May Follow." The San Antonio Daily Light reduced the affair to one line, a "fight between blacks and whites" that "results in no serious wounds."

In early May several German-language papers ran a rewritten version under "Gefährlicher Neger-Mob" that dropped the Coal City sentence and called the attackers "schwarzen Halunken" and the wounded man one of the "wollköpfigen Lümmel." One of them, the Milwaukee Vorwärts, put the attackers at about seventy rather than fifty. No account was found in the Black press, so every version of the affair comes from white papers, and none gives the Black residents' side.

The two accounts differ on who chased the attackers: the wire credited white men with drawn revolvers, while the Indianapolis Journal credited the police. Both were datelined Lawrenceburg rather than Cleves, and neither offers a local or sworn account that would settle the point.

reader.title: Cleves town hall attack and threatened attack on Coal City
bases: The only anti-Black violence the papers describe is an armed white pursuit with gunfire in which one Black man was slightly wounded, and a threatened attack by 'indignant whites' on the Black settlement at Coal City that a patrol was said to be preventing (A1, A3, A4); no attack on the settlement is reported.

The threatened attack on Coal City appears only in one wire dispatch reprinted many times (A1, A2, A3); the Indianapolis Journal's separate special (A4) corroborates the attack on the Cleves hall but does not mention Coal City or a patrol.

accounts.label: Lawrenceburg wire dispatch
accounts.gist: A mob of nearly fifty armed Black men wrecked the Cleves town hall during a white dance; white men with drawn revolvers chased them in a running fight, one Black man was slightly wounded, and a patrol was preventing indignant whites from attacking the Black settlement at Coal City.

accounts.label: Indianapolis Journal special
accounts.gist: At about 1:30 a.m. merrymakers were driven from a reputable dance hall by boulders and met by stones and bullets from a band of nearly fifty Black men, whom police pursued a short distance without taking or recognizing any; the affair was the result of a race war.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the wire unchanged under headlines such as 'Negroes on War Path', 'Mob of Negroes Attacked Town Hall at Cleves' and 'Negro Toughs', presenting the attack on the whites as fact and the threatened reprisal as a closing line.
The Courier-Journal alone headlined the prospect of reprisal: 'Attack on Negro Settlement May Follow.'
The Indianapolis Journal headed its special 'Culmination of a Race War' and called the hall a 'reputable' one.
German-language rewrites called the attackers 'schwarzen Halunken' and the wounded man one of the 'wollköpfigen Lümmel', and dropped the Coal City sentence.

versions.value: White men with drawn revolvers chased the attackers in a running fight
Police pursued them a short distance

conflicts.note: Both reports are datelined Lawrenceburg; neither is a local Cleves account. The accounts may describe different parts of the pursuit.
The 70 appears in one German rewrite whose sister texts say 50; likely a copying or OCR error.
Later papers re-dated the same wire; the Willmar Tribune's 'Thursday morning' and the April 9 'this morning' point to the same day.
